title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
hook: two people who waited a long time recognize the baby in the temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds: the night shift heard the news first, and Mary kept it all. Your line was ponder it in your heart. What moment did you keep? Today the days of Mary and Nazareth come to a close. Day forty-three.

Forty days after a birth, the law of Moses asked a mother to come to the temple, and a firstborn son was presented to God. So Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to Jerusalem. They bring the offering the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The temple courts are loud. Pilgrims, priests, animals, coins changing hands. Nobody is watching a young couple from Galilee with a baby and two birds. Nobody except two people. A widow of great age, and a man who has been waiting a long time, and both of them know what they're looking at. Today, Nunc dimittis.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD.` → `TWO BIRDS, NOT A LAMB.` → `TWO PEOPLE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Luke introduces Simeon in the King James Bible like this: "the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." Waiting for the comfort of his people. Luke says the Spirit had shown him he would not die before he saw the one God promised. So that day he's led into the temple, and he takes the baby in his arms, and he says: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." He calls the child a light for the nations and the glory of Israel. In Latin those first words are Nunc dimittis, now you let go, and Simeon's song has been sung at the end of the day for many centuries: at evening prayer by Anglicans, at night prayer by Catholics, at vespers by Orthodox Christians. Then he turns to Mary with a harder word: a sword will pierce her own soul too. And then Anna. A prophetess, Luke says, very old, married seven years and then a widow, "which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Luke gives a number, eighty-four, and nobody is sure whether it's her age or the years she'd been a widow. She comes up in that same hour, gives thanks, and starts telling everyone who is waiting too. Notice who recognizes the child here. Not the powerful. A man who came when the Spirit led him, and a widow who kept showing up. Luke never gives Simeon's age; painters make him old because he speaks of departing in peace. In Luke's telling, waiting isn't sitting still. It's coming back, day after day, looking.
screen: `JUST AND DEVOUT, WAITING.` · `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART.` · `A SWORD FOR MARY'S SOUL.` · `ANNA, NIGHT AND DAY.` · then, large: `MINE EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of someone older than you who has waited a long time for something. A grandparent who waited for a letter. A neighbor who waited out an illness. Someone still waiting for a phone call from a child. Bring their face to mind. What did the waiting cost them? What did it teach them? Just sit with them for a while. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, honor them quietly in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you let go, the first words of Simeon's song after he held the infant Jesus and said he could depart in peace.

Your line: waiting is not wasted. Today, honor one elder who has waited long: a call, a visit, a real question about their life. Tomorrow the road opens toward Galilee, and it starts with stargazers from the east. Day forty-three.

howItsDone: Many churches keep the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, often called Candlemas, when candles are blessed. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, is sung or said at the close of the day in Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox prayer.

original.note: Greek: waiting for, ready to welcome. Luke's word for Simeon, and for the people Anna spoke to.

trapdoor: what you thought: two minor figures at the edge of the Christmas story.
what it means: two people who waited a lifetime and knew the child when he came, in a crowd where nobody else looked twice.

what a scholar hears: Simeon's song became the Nunc Dimittis, sung at the close of the day east and west, and Luke's Gospel, which opened with an old priest in the temple, brings the story back there, to a widow of great age and a man waiting for consolation.

notes: Closes the Mary and Nazareth block (days 37–43); day 42 already did the week-end look-back, so this day only names the close.

Purification after forty days and the poorer family's offering (Leviticus 12:2–8; Luke 2:22–24). Luke combines purification and presentation of the firstborn (Exodus 13:2, 12); confirm the simplified phrasing.
Anna's age: Luke 2:37 can be read as a widow 'of about fourscore and four years' in age or in length of widowhood; stated as uncertain.
Nunc Dimittis: Evening Prayer (Anglican), Compline (Catholic), Vespers (Orthodox). 'Well over a thousand years' of use at the close of the day; confirm.
'Luke's Gospel opened with an old priest in the temple' refers to Zechariah (Luke 1:8–11); Luke 1:7 says he and Elizabeth were 'well stricken in years'.
Original: προσδεχόμενος (Luke 2:25; cf. 2:38). Confirm form and pronunciation.

Second review (2026-10-01): Luke gives Anna's great age but never Simeon's; 'two very old people' (hook, word, fork, trapdoor, teaser field) now says so, and the teach adds that Luke never gives his age. 'Well over a thousand years' softened to 'many centuries'; 'in the Bible, waiting isn't sitting still' narrowed to Luke; the trapdoor's 'ends its first chapters there' was wrong (chapter 2 continues to the boy in the temple) and is rewritten.
